newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Byron home sale in Geneva nets $2.65 million.
newsitem.headline: Byron home sale in Geneva nets $2.65 million.

text.p: Objects in a Geneva villa where the English poet Lord Byron once lived sold for 3.2 million Swiss francs ($2.65 million) in a two-day auction, Christie's said Thursday.
A 19th-century Russian bronze chandelier, Flemish and Dutch oil paintings, Italian statues, French furniture and a Louis XVI Aubusson tapestry were among the 685 lots finding new owners.

Results for Christie's first house sale in Switzerland were 50 per cent higher than its estimate, it said in a statement on the sale, which ended late Tuesday. Christie's said it was also the highest result in Switzerland for an "on-site" sale.

Byron spent only the summer of 1816 in the Villa Diodati, where he wrote the third canto of his poem "Childe Harold" as well as the "Prisoner of Chillon" after being moved by a visit to the mediaeval castle of the same name near Montreux.
The poet carved his name on a pillar of the castle's damp dungeon which juts into Lake Geneva. The name is still visible, inspiring many tourists to also carve their name into the rock.
Byron's friends Percy and Mary Shelley also lived in Geneva, where Mary Shelley began writing her novel "Frankenstein."

Some 98 percent of the 700 lots found new owners, according to Christie's. An early 19th century bronze Russian chandelier was the top item, going to an unidentified private buyer in the room for 104,700 swiss francs ($85,100), tripling its estimate.

A pair of bronze statues by the early 18th century Venetian sculptor Francesco Bertos sold for 80,500 swiss francs ($65,500). An oil painting by Flemish painter Sebastian Vrancz, entitled Soldiers Ransacking a Village, went for 57,500 Swiss francs ($46,750).
